newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Handelsbanken half year profits up 17 percent.
newsitem.headline: Handelsbanken half year profits up 17 percent.

text.p: Svenska Handelsbanken, Sweden's biggest commercial bank, said profits rose 17 percent in the first half, and hinted it could be a key bidder for the government's stake in mortgage lender Stadshypotek.
Handelsbanken said profits rose to to 3 billion crowns ($456 million) after provisions for loan losses from 2.57 billion crowns ($391 million) posted in the same 1995 period.
The strongest of the Swedish banks during the credit crisis of the early 1990s, Handelsbanken's loan losses did not have as far to fall as those of competitors such as S-E-Banken and Nordbanken.

At 892 million crowns ($136 million), Handelsbanken's net loan losses for the first half of the year were 0.6 percent of total loan volume, near the level commons before the property and banking crises early in the 1990s.
Handelsbanken president Arne Martensson said there was a good chance of loan losses dwindling further.

"Non-performing loans continue to decline, and we have a lower level of non-performers than other (Swedish) banks. This indicates that credit losses will continue falling," Martensson told a news conference.

But falling loan losses were by no means the only source of improved profits for the bank. Higher lending volume led to a 2 percent increase in net interest income to 4.72 billion crowns ($717 million), despite a squeeze on margins from intensifying competition.

A boom year for the Swedish stock market also made its mark on Handelsbanken's results. Commission income rose 29 percent to 1.64 billion crowns ($249 million) on a wave of higher brokerage volumes and corporate finance transactions.
Costs increased by 10 percent, of which three percentage points were attributable to higher depreciation in the leasing operations of the group's financing unit.
With Sweden's commercial banks back on a sound footing, Handelsbanken is expected to be a dominant player as the industry consolidates, industry analysts said.

Freed of the credit losses and the property holdings taken over as collateral during the crisis years, cash-rich Swedish banks are not just potential predators -- their bulging coffers also make them attractive targets.

Handelsbanken is too large a morsel for any other Swedish bank to swallow, analysts said. But Martensson said the bank could be in the bidding for the state's expected sale of its 34 percent holding in Stadshypotek.
"I can't rule out the possibilty that we'll be in the bidding for Stadshypotek," he said, adding that he saw the lender as a natural complement to Handelsbanken's operations in the area.
